# Work on

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
Starts or resumes one work item, plans it, and builds it; it never records an approval, Done, a merge, or a deploy. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. No project briefing in this conversation: run the briefing. Exit code 4: open `project-setup` and stop. Tell the owner each change listed under "Changes found in the tracker", one line each in the CLI's words, before other work.
   `toolkit brief`
2. A bare "ok", "yes", or "looks good" when this chat asked him nothing: start no work and ask what he wants. Otherwise find the item: the id he named, this worktree's item, or a title that matches. Two matches: ask one question naming both.
   `toolkit work list`
   `toolkit work show <id>`
3. No item yet: size the request as a quick edit, log only, or a work item, and pick the type (`references/sizing-and-routing.md`, sections 1 to 3). He asks to be asked first ("ask me questions", "grill me"): open `work-requirements`, which creates the item, and ask nothing here. Otherwise title a new item in his words, say the title in one line, and save his exact words as the Starting request. Log only: reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop.
   `toolkit work new --title '<title>' --type <type> --stage 01-discovery`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Starting request' --text '<his exact words>'`
4. Route by where the item stands: go down the table in `references/sizing-and-routing.md`, section 4, take the first row that matches, and say the route in one line. The owner's decisions come first (`waiting_on: owner` opens `work-decide`). Then the delivery offer: the agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer" for this item, or "you drive", opens `work-delegate`, and nothing is built until he answers. Stay here only for planning and building.
   `toolkit work lifecycle`
5. Plan (stage 06): Roadmap phases and Tasks from the design's Build and verification plan, in the formats in `references/planning.md` (sections 1 to 4).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 06-implementation-plan`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Roadmap --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section Tasks --set-file <file>`
6. Tracking setup (stage 07) when the item changes committed files: its own worktree and branch, with the names the show command prints (`references/git-rules.md` before any Git write).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 07-tracking-setup`
7. Build (stage 08) task by task on the item's branch. Tick a task only with evidence (`references/planning.md`, sections 6 and 7).
   `toolkit work set <id> --stage 08-build`
8. The owner is needed: add an Open Questions row, set the item waiting on him, keep working on what the answer does not block, and ask in the reply (`references/recording-owner-answers.md`).
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | <question> | <affects> | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Last task done: open `work-check`. Stopping with work unfinished: run the checklist in `references/planning.md`, section 8, and end with the one question or the exact words that continue. The final reply repeats every tracker change of this session in the CLI's words: each "Changes found in the tracker" line from step 1, and each "Tell the owner in the reply" line a command printed (a new title, a renamed folder).
   `toolkit work history <id> --note '<what changed>'`
   `toolkit work validate <id>`

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- Setup steps are never work items. They go in the reply, and only a step the doctor command checks also goes in the current focus.
- A deliverable the owner named without its content ("write a short project brief") gets `Q-01` and a question. Never invent the content.
- A change to product behavior, Salesforce metadata, or anything bound for production is `build` (data changes: `data-load`), never `task`, even when it looks small.
- "Ask me questions first" means `work-requirements`, which creates the item. Never ask a batch of questions here.
- Build only on the item's own branch and worktree, never on the default branch. No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): never run `git fetch`.
- A task whose "Done when" names the owner is his question, never ticked by the agent.
- Salesforce: `sf-component-tracker` after each metadata change; production data only through `sf-data-change`. Run each `sf` command directly, never from a script or file you wrote, so the guard sees it. A sandbox deploy or sandbox data change needs the owner's yes for that change; in Codex he runs it himself, so hand him the exact command with its `-o <sandbox>`.

## Agents

- `builder` (`references/agent-builder.md`): one per independent build task, only when `work-delegate` recorded a team or the owner agreed. The main agent merges each builder's branch into the item's branch, then ticks the task. In Codex the main agent first makes each builder's worktree (`references/helpers.md`, section 2, "Codex builders").
- `researcher` (`references/agent-researcher.md`): one per unknown found while planning or building.
- `acceptance-checker` (`references/agent-acceptance-checker.md`): a plan check after step 5 when the plan has several builders, parallel tasks, or a shared environment. Paste in the requirements, the design's Build and verification plan, the Roadmap, and the Tasks.
- Brief them as `references/helpers.md` says; size a team with `references/team-roles.md`.
- Codex: this plugin's agents do not load there. Give the full text of this skill's `references/agent-<name>.md`, with the brief, to a native Codex worker: the `spawn_agent` tool, started without this conversation (`fork_turns` set to `none`), so a checker never shares the builder's thread. With no worker, do the work yourself and say that no independent check ran.

# Keep the Active Work Item Accurate

The work tracker is the source of truth for current work.

- Before substantial work, use the `work-on` skill. Read the active item's requirements, state, next step, and blockers.
- Save the owner's decisions, requirements, and corrections in the item or its linked document before moving on.
- When the work needs the owner's decision, add it to the item's Open Questions with "Decision needed from: owner" and set the item's `waiting_on` to `owner`. The `work-decide` skill records the answer.
- `build` and `data-load` work needs approved requirements before it starts. A later stage does not revoke that approval.
- After the owner accepts agent-led delivery, ask how the team is arranged. That choice authorizes helpers for that goal only.
- Mark an item Done only after the owner approves the result.
- Before ending unfinished work, record the exact next step in the item.

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stages, statuses, and approval gates. "Where information goes" in `AGENTS.md` is the routing table; the `work-delegate` skill holds the delivery offer and team questions, and the `handoff` skill holds the handoff steps.

# Humanize Anything Sent to Another Person

Any text that will leave the project and be read by someone other than the owner
is run through the `humanizer` skill before the owner sees the final version.
Use the `unslop` skill when `humanizer` is not installed. That covers emails,
chat messages, support case text and comments, GitHub issues, pull request
descriptions, client documents, and any file made to hand to someone else.

Keep every fact, name, id, number, and date exactly as it was. Write it in the
owner's voice, first person, when it goes out under their name.

It does not apply to chat replies to the owner, work items, project knowledge,
code, or commit messages.

# Review and Save Project Memory

This rule applies to the main agent. The project memory system is chosen at setup and recorded in `.toolkit.json`; with built-in memory it is the local `.memory/` folder. It is the single project memory store. Claude's native auto-memory and the `claude-toolkit` Second Brain plugin are disabled for this project. The session-start briefing shows the current focus in Claude Code and Codex. Do not treat a hook reminder as a save decision.

## Decide the destination first

Read the memory criteria (`.memory/memory-criteria.md` with built-in memory) and the likely owning record. Send current focuses, owner to-dos, and handoff context to the current focus; sourced terminology to the glossary; qualifying otherwise-unowned durable context to a topic; active work to the chosen tracker; decisions for the whole project to `DECISIONS.md`; accepted delivered behavior to requirements; the technical approach to the design kept with its work item; verified current structure to the System Guide; and repeatable procedure to instructions or a skill. Raw external documentation stays in its source folder. A small memory pointer can route future sessions to a hard-to-find authority without copying its body.

Review on explicit remember/forget requests, corrections, standing preferences, meaningful decisions or discoveries, significant fixes or episodes, people/tool/reference changes, focus shifts, work-item completion, and handoffs. The toolkit's `UserPromptSubmit` hook flags only explicit keep phrases, and its Stop hook checks once per turn that such a phrase was handled. Do not save on every hook reminder or every turn. A review can end with no memory.

## Approval

The `memory-save` skill holds the approval policy: what the owner's own words authorize, what needs a yes in onboarding mode, what trusted mode allows, and what always needs the owner. The mode is `memory.approval` in `.toolkit.json`; only an explicit owner instruction changes it. A yes authorizes the shown operation and meaning only. Silence does not. An unanswered save question is kept as a proposal: the agent does not rely on it, and `work-decide` shows it to the owner until he approves or rejects it. The `memory-save` skill says how.

If the owner says a proposed item should not be memory, withdraw it. Save only a general selection rule, as a `feedback` memory, if their feedback supplies one; do not restate the rejected fact in the current focus or another topic. Review similar candidates against that rule from then on.

## Saving and completion

The main agent saves memory itself through the `memory-save` skill, which runs `toolkit memory` commands; there is no curator agent. Search first with `toolkit memory find`, then save with `toolkit memory save`, retire with `toolkit memory retire`, and write the current focus or glossary with `toolkit memory focus --set-file` or `toolkit memory glossary --set-file`. The commands lock memory, refuse stale edits, and rebuild the index.

For a focus-only change or already-authorized glossary maintenance, save without a lasting-memory question. Several independent signals can be grouped into one save; do not run parallel writes against the same topic or index. Before claiming a save succeeded, read it back with `toolkit memory get` and run `toolkit doctor`; tell the user briefly what was retained or what needs a decision.

# Prepare a Session Handoff

When the owner says he is clearing context or ending the session, or asks for a handoff, use the `handoff` skill, whatever the session's length. When the session is long and the next step is complex, offer a handoff. Use the `handoff` skill. Before the handoff, review the current focus (`toolkit memory focus`) and the memory criteria; update the focus, and save only authorized lasting memory, with the `memory-save` skill. Then write the prompt. Skip the offer for small edits and quick lookups.

# Work Safely in a Shared Repository

Other sessions edit this repository now. Before your first edit, run:

```
git worktree list
git status
git fetch origin && git log --oneline -10
```

- No remote (`git remote` prints nothing): skip `git fetch`, and never report a fetch failure as a blocker.
- An unknown worktree, moved branch, or change you did not make means other sessions are live. Do not fix it. Tell the owner.
- Code, rules, skills, hooks, settings: use your own worktree and branch (`git worktree add .claude/worktrees/<name> -b claude/<name>`). Exception: a one-file edit asked for directly.
- Documentation-only saves: open the `publish-docs` skill.
- In the shared primary checkout, never switch branches, reset, rebase, or stash.
- Never touch another session's branch or uncommitted work.
- Stage paths by name. Never `git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`. Read the full staged diff.
- Never hand-edit a generated file.
- Before taking a sequential number, check every tracker folder, worktree, and the remote. On a later collision, renumber only your own.
- Land implementation by pull request, merged with the owner's approval. A standing merge instruction the owner gave for this project counts.
- Before a merge, compare `git diff --name-only <default-branch>...<branch>` with `git status` in the primary checkout. A file in both: stop, name it, ask the owner.
- After the merge, remove your worktree and branch.

# Write Artifacts in Plain English

An artifact is something an agent generates for a person to look at: a
diagram, a chart, a dashboard, a visualization, a mockup, a slide deck, a
published page, or a generated document. This rule is about the words inside
one: the title, the headings, the labels, the notes, the captions, the body
text.

The project's output style says how the agent talks in chat. The words inside
an artifact follow the same style. This rule exists because the output style
reaches only the main chat: a helper agent, a skill, or a Codex session that
makes an artifact never sees it. Read the active style file when there is
one. Where this rule and that file differ, the style file wins.

## Write about the subject

Every word describes the thing the artifact shows. The reader opened it to
learn about that thing, not about the artifact or the conversation that
produced it.

- Do not narrate the artifact. "Here is where the change lands, but only the
  key pieces" says nothing about the system. Cut it, or say what changed.
- Do not tell the reader what matters. "Here is the load-bearing decision"
  tells them how to feel. Write the decision.
- Bring in the conversation only when it is the fact. A quote earns its place
  when the exact words are what the reader needs, and then it says who said
  it and when. A quote the reader cannot place is noise.

## A heading names what is under it

A heading is a label, not a hook. It says what the reader is about to look
at, in the words of the subject.

The four headings below are an example: a page of options for who can see and
edit which projects in a team web app. The left column sells the section; the
right column names it.

| Written | Say instead |
|---|---|
| Three ways to build the team tree, pick one | Team structure options |
| One question decides the whole shape | Decision: can a team lead edit their own team's projects? |
| Four facts that rule out the most obvious answers | How team access works |
| What shape actually hands to a real person | Project visibility by role |

A number belongs in a heading when the number is the fact: "Three departments
share one role". "Three ways to build it" only counts the section below, and
the reader can count.

## Use the real name

Call a thing what the system calls it, every time. In that example the real
names are team structure, project visibility, sharing rule, admin access, and
permission group. The page used picture words instead: "shape" for the team
structure, "lever" for a setting, "leaks" for access people should not have,
"flows up" for a manager getting access to their team's projects. That is
figurative language, and it is not allowed. It makes the reader translate, and
a reader who does not know the system cannot.

A term the reader may not know gets a plain definition the first time it
appears. After that, the term is used unchanged.

A box or label carries the real name. Anything it needs to say about itself
is one plain line.

## Say the plain thing

Use the active output style inside the artifact. This artifact rule also requires:

- Common words. Short sentences. One idea each.
- No figurative or metaphorical language. No idioms, no jokes, no picture word
  standing in for a real thing.
- No preamble. Start with the content.
- No closing line that sums up or cheers.
- Fewer words, never fewer facts. Every number, name, date, and quotation
  stays exactly as it is.

## What this rule does not decide

How the artifact is laid out: how many boxes, what an arrow says, where a
note goes, whether there is a key. Every artifact is different, and the agent
making it decides. This rule decides the words.

# Sizing a request and routing an item

How `work-on` decides between a quick edit, a logged item, and a worked item,
which type to give it, and which skill continues it.

## Contents

1. Three sizes of request
2. Owner messages and the right action
3. Choosing the type
4. Routing by where the item stands
5. Several items at once
6. Project roadmap units

## 1. Three sizes of request

- **Quick edit, no item.** One sitting, no choice for the owner, no change to
  behavior recorded in `requirements/`, nothing bound for production. Do it
  and report it in one line.
- **Log only.** The owner says "later", "backlog", "park that", "not now", or
  "log a bug". Check the list for a duplicate, create the item at
  `01-discovery` with his exact words as the Starting request, reply
  "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." and stop.
- **Work item.** Everything else. "New work", "track", "work item", or "done
  properly" always makes an item. A request that grows past a quick edit
  while you work becomes an item then, with his words as the Starting
  request.

Never make a work item for project setup. Setup steps the owner must do go in
the reply. Only a step `toolkit doctor` checks (trusting the hooks in Codex
`/hooks`, `ntn login`) also goes in the current focus under "Waiting on the
owner", marked as a setup step, and leaves it once doctor stops reporting it.
"Start a new session" goes in the reply only.

A deliverable the owner named without saying what it should say or do ("write
a short project brief"): create the item, add the content question as `Q-01`
with the item waiting on him, and ask it in the reply before building.
Never invent the content.

## 2. Owner messages and the right action

| The owner says | Right action |
| --- | --- |
| "Fix the typo in the README heading." | Quick edit. Fix it, say what changed in one line. No item. |
| "What does the export function do?" | Answer the question. No item. |
| "Log a bug: the export drops the last row. Not now." | Log only: check for a duplicate, create a `bug` item at `01-discovery` with his words, reply "Logged as WI-014 (bug, backlog). Not started." |
| "Add a CSV export to the monthly report." | Work item, type `build`. Create it, then route: requirements are not approved, so open `work-requirements`. |
| "Write a short project brief." | Work item, type `task`. Add `Q-01` "What should the brief cover?", set it waiting on the owner, ask the question. |
| "Keep going." (no item named) | Continue this worktree's item, or the item the current focus says the next session starts with, or the one `toolkit work next` recommends. Say which in one line. |
| "ok" (and this chat asked him nothing) | Not "keep going". Start no work; ask what he wants. |
| "Ask me questions first, then build it." | Create the item and open `work-requirements` for the interview. Never batch questions here. |
| "Put it in the backlog and I'll tell you when." | Log only. |
| "WI-007" or "resume WI-007" | Read WI-007 and route it by where it stands (section 4). |

## 3. Choosing the type

- Pick the closest type from `toolkit work lifecycle`.
- A change to what the product does, to Salesforce metadata (`force-app/`),
  or to anything bound for production is `build`, never `task`, even when it
  looks small. A change to data is `data-load`.
- `build` and `data-load` need the owner's requirements approval before stage
  03. The CLI refuses a later stage without it.
- A `task` with no open choices may skip the requirements approval and go
  straight to planning. Put the reason in a history note.

## 4. Routing by where the item stands

The "Continue with" line of `toolkit work show <id>` is the default. The
item's real state decides. Go down the table in order and take the first row
that matches: the owner's waiting decisions come first, then the delivery
offer, then the stage. Say the route in one line.

| Where the item stands | Open | One-line announcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `waiting_on: owner` | `work-decide` (ask that one question first; keep working on anything it does not block) | "WI-012 is waiting for your OK on the requirements." |
| The agent to-do "Make the agent-led delivery offer" for this item (the briefing and `toolkit work decisions` list it for a big top-level item at stages 03 to 07 that still has `delivery: not-offered`), or the owner hands the goal over ("you drive") | `work-delegate`, and build nothing until he answers | "WI-012 needs your delivery choice; opening work-delegate." |
| Requirements not approved and type `build` or `data-load` | `work-requirements` | "WI-012 needs requirements first; opening work-requirements." |
| The owner asks to change, add, or drop a requirement, at any stage | `work-requirements` | "That changes R-02; opening work-requirements." |
| Requirements approved, more than one reasonable way to build, no approved design | `solution-design` | "WI-012 needs a design; opening solution-design." |

# Work delegate

Voice: write to the owner in plain English. Claude Code: follow the project's Plain English output style. Codex: follow the "How to write replies" section of `AGENTS.md`.
The only skill that makes the agent-led delivery offer and records the answer; after a yes it runs the team through the skill that owns each stage. Track these steps with the host's plan tool (Claude Code: the task list; Codex: `update_plan`), not in the reply.

## Steps

1. Look for a delivery choice that covers this goal: the item's `delivery` value, its Notes > Decisions and context, and its parent's choice. A sub-item makes no offer. A quick question, a small edit, or a small item (one or two tasks, no sub-items) gets no offer: record owner-led with the reason and go on (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 1).
   `toolkit work show <id> --section 'Decisions and context'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'`
2. No choice recorded: add the offer as an Open Questions row, set the item waiting on the owner, and ask exactly this as the last line of the reply: "Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?" "You drive" in his own words is already the answer.
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
3. Yes: ask the team question. Where the host lets this chat list, read, and message other chats and offer new chats to the owner: "Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?" On any other host, say the multi-chat arrangement is not available here and ask: "Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?"
4. Main Orchestrator chosen: also ask "Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?"
5. Record the choice, the goal it covers, who said it, the date, the team arrangement, the archive answer, and the limits in Notes > Decisions and context; set the delivery value; hand the item back to the agent unless another of his questions is open; add one history note; read it back (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 3).
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Decisions and context' --set-file <file>`
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
   `toolkit work history <id> --note 'Agent-led delivery accepted by <owner>: <his words>'`
6. No, or a later revoke: record it the same way, and set `waiting_on` to `agent` when the agent still works on the item. Do not offer again for this goal unless it grows a lot or the owner asks.
   `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led`
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`
7. Run the team through the skill that owns each stage (`references/agent-led-delivery.md`, section 4; `references/team-arrangements.md`). The main agent plans, briefs the helpers, gives one writer per path, and is the only writer of the work item.
   `toolkit work list --tree`
8. Stop at every owner gate: set the item waiting on him and ask through the skill that owns the gate. Keep working on what the answer does not block.
   `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner`
9. Archive a chat only when its task is complete, merged and shipped, its report is saved, the owner approved it, and he said yes to archiving. Never delete a chat.
10. End every reply with the one question (the offer, the team question, or the next gate) or the exact words that continue ("Say 'go' and the team starts on P1.").

## Gotchas

- Run each `toolkit` command alone: never joined by `&&`, `;`, or a pipe, and never from a script (in Codex that runs it inside the sandbox, where it fails). One-line values go in single quotes, never double quotes; an apostrophe inside them is `'\''` in Claude Code and ’ (U+2019) in Codex, or reword the text. Section text goes on standard input (`--set-file -`) in Claude Code, and in `--text '<text>'` or a `mktemp -d` file in Codex (`references/toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
- The offer and the team questions are asked word for word, in the reply text, never through a question tool.
- The `--delivery` command marks the offer's Open Questions row Answered and prints "Marked Q-xx Answered". Never edit that row by hand. When no other question for him is open, it also sets `waiting_on` to `none` ("It is no longer waiting on the owner"). Set `agent` right after it when the agent continues (steps 5 and 6); keep `owner` while another of his questions on the item is open.
- A sub-item is part of its parent's goal: creating it under the parent copies the parent's delivery value. Set it only when it is missing or differs, with a note naming the parent.
- The choice belongs to the named goal only. It does not carry over to another goal, a new item, or an unrelated sub-item.
- Acceptance alone starts no helpers; the team arrangement answer does. A no to the team question means no helpers.
- Delegation never widens merge, deployment, spending, or publishing. Every approval gate still applies, and approvals already given still count.
- Missing tracker access is not a missing decision. Keep an unsaved choice in the handoff and save it when access returns.
- A recorded lead or chat id is coordination information, not proof that an agent is still running.
- GitHub Issues or Jira: `toolkit work` exits with code 3. Record the choice in the issue's Notes and a delivery label (`references/tracker-github.md` or `references/tracker-jira.md`).

# Agent-led delivery

The rules for the delivery offer: when to make it, the exact questions, how
to record the owner's answers, and what an acceptance allows. The four
questions keep their exact wording. The choice is recorded in the work item's
Notes > Decisions and context and in its `delivery` value, in every tracker.

## Contents

1. Offer once for the goal
2. Ask how the team is arranged
3. Record the choice
4. Divide responsibility

## 1. Offer once for the goal

First read the item's `delivery` value and its Notes > Decisions and context
to see whether the owner already accepted, declined, or revoked agent-led
delivery for this goal. `not-offered` means no answer is recorded yet. Do not
treat missing access as an undecided choice. When the records show no choice,
ask exactly:

> Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner?

`work-delegate` is the only skill that makes this offer or records its
answer. `work-on`, `work-decide`, and the session briefing only point at it,
so the owner is asked once, in one place.

Do not make this offer for a simple question or quick edit, or for a small
item (one or two tasks, no sub-items): record owner-led at once, with the
reason, so the briefing stops listing the offer as an agent to-do.

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led --note 'Small item: one or two tasks, so no delivery offer.'
```

The offer is made once, at the top item of the goal; a sub-item is part of
its parent's goal. `toolkit work new --parent` copies the parent's delivery
value to a new sub-item and says so ("Delivery: agent-led, as recorded for
WI-012."). Check it, and make no offer for it. Only when the value is missing
or differs from the parent's, set it with a note naming the parent:

```text
toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led --note 'Part of WI-012, whose goal is agent-led.'
```

When you ask, first add the question as an Open Questions row (owner decides,
Affects `delivery`) and set the item waiting on the owner, so a later session
sees the offer is open if the answer does not come in this one:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| <next Q-id> | Would you like agents to take responsibility for delivering this, with you acting as product owner? | delivery | Open | owner |'
toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on owner
```

Ask it in the reply text, as its last line, never through a question tool.
Wait for the answer before taking responsibility for organizing delivery,
while continuing any useful work that does not depend on the choice. The
`--delivery` command that records his answer marks that row Answered and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit the row by hand.

A clear acceptance authorizes agent-led delivery for this goal across
sessions. A later explicit request for agents to manage or deliver the goal
also counts ("you drive", "run with it", "take it from here"); do not ask the
offer question again. A decline keeps normal help and the usual record upkeep,
and stops the offer for this goal, including in later sessions. Offer again
only if the work grows a lot or the owner asks about agent-led delivery. The
owner may revoke acceptance at any time. Record it as revoked: agent-led
responsibility ends, normal help and record upkeep continue, and the same
rules as a decline apply.

The choice belongs to the named goal. It does not carry over to an unrelated
goal, a new work item, or an unrelated sub-item. The end of a session does not
end it, and missing tracker access does not mean the owner is undecided.

## 2. Ask how the team is arranged

After a clear acceptance, read the goal record for a saved team arrangement.
When none is recorded, ask one more question:

> Do you want one team inside this chat, or do you want me to rename this chat to Main Orchestrator and coordinate other chats that each have their own team?

Offer the multi-chat choice only where the current host lets this chat list,
read, and message other chats and offer new chats to the owner as task
buttons. Check the tools this session has; do not assume. On any other host,
tell the owner the multi-chat arrangement is not available on this host and
ask one simple question instead:

> Shall I run one team of helpers inside this chat?

A yes is an arrangement choice: one team inside this chat. A no means the main
agent does the work itself. Record either answer with the goal.

Do not ask after a decline or a revocation, and do not ask again once the
owner's answer is recorded for the goal. The owner may change the arrangement
at any time; record the new answer.

When the owner chooses the Main Orchestrator arrangement, ask one more
question:

> Do you want me to archive sessions after their task is fully complete, everything is merged and shipped, and you approved?

Record the answer with the goal like the arrangement answer, and do not ask it
again.

`team-arrangements.md` explains what each answer means, including when a
chat may be archived. Read it before organizing the team, and when resuming a
goal that has a recorded arrangement.

## 3. Record the choice

Save accepted, declined, or revoked, and the team arrangement answer once
given, in the item:

- `toolkit work set <id> --delivery agent-led` for accepted;
  `toolkit work set <id> --delivery owner-led` for declined or revoked.
- When the offer's row was his last open question, the delivery command
  also sets `waiting_on` to `none` and prints "It is no longer waiting on the
  owner". When the agent continues the item (an acceptance, or a decline
  with work still to do), set it to `agent`:
  `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on agent`. Keep `owner` while another of
  his questions on the item is open.
- A block in Notes > Decisions and context, written with
  `toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Decisions and context' --set-file <file>`:

  ```markdown
  - **Agent-led delivery (WI-012 goal: CSV export):** accepted by Mike on
    2026-09-26 ("you drive, I'll approve things"). Team: one team inside this
    chat. Archive answer: not asked. Limits: no merge, deployment, spending, or
    publishing beyond what was given. Lead: this chat.
  ```

- One history note with the owner's words.

Record the goal scope, the state (accepted, declined, or revoked), the team
arrangement answer when one was given, the archive answer when it was asked,
who said it and the date, the limits, and which chat or agent leads delivery.
A lead reference coordinates ownership; it is not a lock and not proof that an
agent is still running. Read the saved section back and check the meaning
landed.

Keep the Overview Next action consistent with the choice. For example,
replace a pending "ask whether agents lead" next action once the owner

With acceptance, agents take responsibility for moving the agreed goal

Run each stage through the skill that owns it: `work-requirements`,

# Running `toolkit` commands

Purpose: how to run a `toolkit` command in Claude Code and in Codex, how to
pass text in one, and what each exit code means. Every skill that runs a
`toolkit` command follows this file.

## Contents

- Running toolkit commands
- Text in a command
- Exit codes
- Reporting a save
- Reading output and updating what you read
- Right and wrong examples

## Running toolkit commands

- Put each `toolkit` command on its own line and run it as a plain command,
  in both hosts. Do not join it to another command with `&&`, `;`, or a pipe,
  and do not wrap it in `$(...)`, a loop, or a script. This holds for read
  commands too: `toolkit work decisions && toolkit work show WI-001` is two
  commands, run one after the other.
- Why, in Codex: the project's command rule (`.codex/rules/toolkit.rules`)
  runs a `toolkit` command outside the sandbox only when it is the whole
  command. A `toolkit` command joined to anything else (`&&`, `;`, a pipe, a
  heredoc, `cd ... &&`) or run from a script (for example Python's
  `subprocess`) runs inside the Codex sandbox. The sandbox blocks Notion, the
  local Hindsight server, and the main checkout's `.work-items/` and
  `.memory/` from a worktree, so the command fails or reports the wrong
  cause.
- The one thing a Claude Code command may carry is its own text on standard
  input (`--set-file -` with a quoted heredoc; "Text in a command", below).
- Five commands ask the owner first, in both hosts, because they are hard or
  impossible to undo: `toolkit machine-setup`, `toolkit memory delete`,
  `toolkit memory import`, `toolkit import`, and
  `toolkit hindsight service install` or `start`. Get his yes in the reply
  before you run one. The host then asks him to confirm the command (Claude
  Code: a permission prompt; Codex: an approval). That prompt is expected, not
  an error.
- In Codex, run each of those five alone, with `sandbox_permissions` set to
  `require_escalated` and a one-line reason. The approval alone keeps the
  command inside the sandbox, where it fails: `toolkit memory delete` cannot
  reach Hindsight or Notion, `toolkit machine-setup` cannot write `~/.codex`
  or `~/.local/bin`, `toolkit hindsight service install` cannot write
  `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, and `toolkit import` from a worktree cannot write
  the main checkout.
- Write `--json` and `--host` after the command words
  (`toolkit memory delete <key> --owner-approved --json`). The toolkit refuses
  those five commands when a flag comes first, because the ask-first rules
  would not match them.
- Never change a work item or a memory record with a script or a shell write
  (Python, Node, `sed -i`, `cat >`, `tee`, `cp`). Use the `toolkit` command
  that owns it. The hooks refuse the shell write, so it only wastes a step.
- `toolkit help <command>` prints every option of one command.

## Text in a command

The shell changes text before the command sees it. Inside double quotes it
runs anything between backticks and anything in `$(...)` as a command, and
puts that command's output in the text. The command then saves the text with
those parts missing and still reports success. So:

- **One-line values** (`--note`, `--effect`, `--append-row`, `--title`,
  `--reason`, `--quote`, `--evidence`, `--description`, `--source`): put them
  in single quotes, in both hosts. Inside single quotes the shell changes
  nothing. Never use double quotes for text.
- **An apostrophe inside single quotes:**
  - Claude Code: write it as `'\''`, for example
    `--note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`.
  - Codex: write it as ’ (the curly apostrophe, U+2019), or reword the text.
    Never `'\''` in Codex: the command rule does not match that form, so the
    command runs inside the sandbox, and the tool call can drop the
    backslash, which leaves a quote that is never closed.
- **Section, design, focus, glossary, and memory text in Claude Code:** pass
  it on standard input with `--set-file -` (or `--body-file -` for a memory
  save) and a quoted heredoc. The quotes around `EOF` in `<<'EOF'` stop the
  shell from changing anything in the text, and no file is left anywhere.
  Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary file there
  could never be deleted. Write the command, then the text, then a line
  holding only `EOF`:

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --set-file - <<'EOF'
  <the whole section text>
  EOF
  ```

- **The same text in Codex:** a heredoc runs the command inside the sandbox,
  so do not use one. Give short or medium text in single quotes
  (`--text '<text>'`; newlines inside the quotes are kept). For longer text:
  1. Make a new folder for this one save with `mktemp -d`. Its name is
     unique, so two sessions or two projects never share a file.
  2. Write the file in it with the file edit tool (`apply_patch`).
  3. Run the `toolkit` command alone, with the file's full path.
  4. Delete the file and the folder right after the command succeeds
     (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`), before you ask the owner anything.

  Never write the file and run the `toolkit` command in one shell command.

  ```text
  toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'
  toolkit work design <id> --text '<text>' --status proposed
  toolkit memory focus --text '<text>' --expect <version>
  ```

- Never use a fixed file name such as `/tmp/wi001-requirements.md`. Every
  project starts at `WI-001`, so another session's save could land in this
  item.
- Never leave a draft file inside `.work-items/` or `.memory/`. A second
  `DESIGN.md`-shaped file there confuses the design lookup, and a stray note
  in `.memory/` is read as a memory.

## Exit codes

`toolkit help work` prints them as: "0 ok, 1 error, 2 validation failure or a
refused gate, 3 not supported for this tracker, 4 not a toolkit project."
`toolkit help memory` uses the same numbers: "1 error or not found, 2 refused
(a rule or a stale --expect), 3 not supported by this backend".

| Code | Meaning | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | Done. | Read back what you wrote before you report it as saved ("Reporting a save", below). A "Note:" line in the output still needs action: report it to the owner, or do what it says. |
| `1` | Error, or the record was not found. | Read the message. It names the cause and usually the fix. Do not run the same command again unchanged. |
| `2` | Validation failure, a refused gate, or a stale `--expect`. | Fix what the message names and run the command again. A refused gate means an approval is missing: ask the owner for it. Never work around a refusal. |
| `3` | Not supported for this tracker or memory backend. | For a GitHub or Jira tracker, the message prints the path of the written instructions for that tracker. Follow them to make the same change on the issue. |
| `4` | Not a Toolkit V2 project. | Skip every work item and memory step and say so in one line. To set the project up, open the `project-setup` skill. |

`toolkit: command not found` means this computer cannot reach the command.
The `project-setup` skill fixes that.

## Reporting a save

- Save each settled answer before moving on, then read it back. A command
  that exits `0` is not proof by itself.
- A write failed: lead the reply with "Not saved". Name what was not saved
  and where it should go, and keep the text so it can be saved later.
- "Saved but not verified" in the output means the write happened and the
  read-back failed. The message names the first part that differs. Lead the
  reply with "Saved but not verified", say which part, and read the record
  back to judge it.

## Reading output and updating what you read

- Add `--json` when you need to read the output field by field, for example
  a record's `version`.
- `--expect <version>` tells the command which version of a record you read.
  The command refuses the save (exit `2`) when the record changed since then,
  so you never overwrite a newer edit. Read it again, merge, and save with the
  new version. `toolkit memory focus`, `toolkit memory glossary`, and
  `toolkit memory save` take it. `--expect absent` says it must not exist
  yet: a new record, or a project with no focus yet.

## Right and wrong examples

1. Two reads.
   - Wrong: `toolkit work list && toolkit work show WI-004`
   - Right: `toolkit work list`, then, as a second command,
     `toolkit work show WI-004`.
2. A history note that quotes the owner, with an apostrophe in his words.
   - Wrong: ``toolkit work history WI-004 --note "Owner said: it's ready, `ship it`"``
     (double quotes: the shell runs the words between the backticks as a
     command and saves its output in their place).
   - Right in Claude Code:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it'\''s ready, ship it"'`
   - Right in Codex:
     `toolkit work history WI-004 --note 'Owner said: "it’s ready, ship it"'`
   - The prefix is `Owner said:`, which has no apostrophe to escape.
3. Section text in Codex.
   - Wrong: `cat > /tmp/overview.md <<'EOF' ... EOF && toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --set-file /tmp/overview.md`
     (one shell command, a heredoc, and a fixed file name).
   - Right: `toolkit work edit WI-004 --section 'Overview' --text '<text>'`
4. A change to a work item's header.
   - Wrong: `sed -i '' 's/^stage: .*/stage: 04-solution-design/' .work-items/WI-004/WORK-ITEM.md`
   - Right: `toolkit work set WI-004 --stage 04-solution-design --note '<why>'`
5. Toolkit commands from a script.
   - Wrong: `for id in WI-001 WI-002; do toolkit work show $id; done`
   - Right: `toolkit work show WI-001`, then `toolkit work show WI-002`, each
     as its own command.

# Work item and design format

What a work item and its design hold, their exact section names, and how to
change them with `toolkit work` commands without losing text.

## Contents

1. Where the record and the design live
2. Header fields
3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`
4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`
5. Finding an item's file
6. Changing one section
7. Adding a table row
8. Editing a record directly
9. Titles
10. Generated files
11. Examples

## 1. Where the record and the design live

Every tracker uses the same body and the same design shape. Only the place
differs.

| Tracker | Work item | Design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local | `WORK-ITEM.md` in the item's folder under `.work-items/` | `DESIGN.md` beside it |
| Notion | The item's page in the project's Work Items database | The item's "Solution Design" child page |
| GitHub Issues | The issue body | One issue comment whose first line is `## Solution design` |
| Jira | The issue description | One comment whose first line is "Solution design" |

An item has one design home. Never make a separate design folder or a second
design file.

## 2. Header fields

The header (frontmatter locally, properties in Notion) holds these fields.
Only `toolkit work` commands change them.

| Field | Values | Changed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `WI-001` (the project's prefix and a number) | `toolkit work new`; never reused |
| `title` | The owner's words for the request | `toolkit work set <id> --title` |
| `type` | `discovery`, `solution-design`, `build`, `data-load`, `repository-maintenance`, `research`, `task`, `bug`, `enhancement`, or another lower-case word | `toolkit work set <id> --type` |
| `stage` | `01-discovery` to `14-spec-update` | `toolkit work set <id> --stage`, `approve`, `finish`, `cancel` |
| `status` | Backlog, Ready, In Progress, In Review, Done, Cancelled | Follows the stage; Done and Cancelled only through `finish` and `cancel` |
| `parent` | An item id or `none` | `toolkit work new --parent`, `toolkit work move` |
| `waiting_on` | `owner`, `agent`, `external: <who>`, `none` | `toolkit work set <id> --waiting-on` |
| `priority` | `urgent`, `high`, `medium`, `low` | `toolkit work set <id> --priority` |
| `delivery` | `agent-led`, `owner-led`, `not-offered` | `toolkit work set <id> --delivery` |
| `requirements_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --requirements` |
| `design` | `proposed`, `approved`, `superseded`, `none` | `toolkit work design`, `toolkit work approve <id> --design` |
| `result_approved` | `YYYY-MM-DD by <name>` or `no` | `toolkit work approve <id> --result`, `toolkit work finish --quote` |
| `updated` | `YYYY-MM-DD` | Every `toolkit work` write |

`toolkit work lifecycle` prints the stage labels, the statuses, and the types.
Blocked is not a status: an item that cannot move has `waiting_on` set and its
Overview Blockers line filled.

## 3. Sections of `WORK-ITEM.md`

These are the headings `--section` takes. A `###` subsection can be named on
its own, for example `--section 'Agreed goal'`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `Overview` | Goal, Current position, Next action (and who owns it), Blockers, Related items (ids, never paths) |
| `Roadmap` | The phase table: Phase (`P1 — <name>`), Outcome, Status, Exit result, Sub-items |
| `Tasks` | One `### P1 — <name>` heading per phase, with checkbox tasks `P1-T01` (Work, Deliverable, Done when, Depends on) |
| `Recent History` | Dated rows: Date, Change or decision, Effect on the work (newest first) |
| `Open Questions` | Rows: ID (`Q-01`), Question, Affects, Status, Decision needed from (`owner` for the owner) |
| `Requirements` | Overall status and Finalization rule, then the subsections below |
| `Starting request` | The owner's own words for the request |
| `Agreed goal` | The outcome the owner agreed the item delivers |
| `Active requirements` | One `#### R-01 — <name>` block per requirement |
| `Acceptance` | The numbered list of what makes the whole item acceptable |
| `Notes` | The subsections below |
| `Decisions and context` | Context the next session needs that is not a requirement |
| `Resume here` | Where the next session picks up |
| `Solution options and considerations` | Build ideas, linked to an `R-xx`; never requirements |

The `R-xx` block fields are Status (Refining, Finalized, Superseded), Applies
to, Required behavior, Boundaries and exceptions, Acceptance check, Decision
record, and Open questions. Each field starts its own line.

In the local and Notion trackers, the requirements approval command sets the
Requirements "Overall status" line: never write that line by hand there.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Finalized there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`,
"The `toolkit work` steps").

## 4. Sections of `DESIGN.md`

The CLI writes the design's header fields: `work_item`, `status` (`proposed`,
`approved`, `superseded`), and `approved`.

| Heading | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Header lines | Requirements (the item id), Design status, Requirements checked, Last updated, Design approval |
| `What this design solves` | Who uses the result, what they need, what must be true afterward, and what is left to another item |
| `Requirements and design readiness` | One row per `R-xx`: its status in the item, the design coverage, the remaining decision or gap |
| `What exists today` | Verified current behavior and files, or "nothing exists yet" |
| `Constraints and assumptions` | One row each, with source, status, and effect on the design |
| `Design options` | `### Option A — <name>` (then B, C), each with Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order |
| `Option comparison` | Only with more than one option |
| `Recommendation and owner decision` | Recommendation, Owner decision, Reason for decision |
| `Selected design` | After the owner chooses: End-to-end flow; Components and responsibilities; Data, access, and integration details; Edge cases and failure behavior; Release and ongoing operation |
| `Diagrams` | Mermaid diagrams, each with a heading and a one-sentence explanation |
| `Build and verification plan` | Technical sequence, and Acceptance checks (one row per requirement) |
| `Sources and decisions that affect the build` | Claim or decision, source, date, evidence type, how it was checked |
| `Where a builder could misread this design` | Requirement or section, plausible wrong reading, intended reading |
| `Notes` | Open design questions, Design changes during the interview, Current position and next step |

Keep every heading exactly as the template has it, including the dash in
`Option A — <name>`. In the local and Notion trackers, never write "Approved"
in the Design status line: a save replaces that line with the stored status,
and only `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` approves a design.
GitHub Issues and Jira have no approve command, so after the owner's yes the
agent writes Approved there itself (`tracker-github.md` or `tracker-jira.md`).

## 5. Finding an item's file

Never build a path by hand. The owner may have moved or renamed the folder.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --path
```

`toolkit work show <id>` also prints the item's stage, who it waits on, the
skill that continues it, its parent and sub-items, its design (or the
parent's approved design it inherits), and the worktree branch and folder to
use.

## 6. Changing one section

1. Read the section. The output is the whole section as it stands.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`
2. Change only what needs to change. Keep the rest word for word.
3. Leave out the section's fill-in guide comment (`<!-- ... -->`) once the
   section holds real content.
4. Write the whole section back. `<file>` is `-` in Claude Code, with the text
   on standard input; in Codex use `--text '<text>'` or a file in a new
   `mktemp -d` folder (`toolkit-commands.md`, "Text in a command").
   `toolkit work edit <id> --section '<heading>' --set-file <file>`
5. Read it back. An exit code of `0` is not proof by itself.
   `toolkit work show <id> --section '<heading>'`

To remove the template's fill-in guide above Overview:

```text
toolkit work edit <id> --remove-guide
```

## 7. Adding a table row

Add one row to Open Questions or Recent History with `--append-row` and the
full Markdown row in single quotes.

A new question takes the next free `Q-` number: read the Open Questions
section first and add one to the highest number there (`Q-01` when there is
none). "Decision needed from" is `owner` for the owner, or a person or role.

```text
toolkit work show <id> --section 'Open Questions'
toolkit work edit <id> --section 'Open Questions' --append-row '| Q-03 | Should the export include archived rows? | R-02 | Open | owner |'
```

A history row is added with its own command, which writes the date:

```text
toolkit work history <id> --note '<what happened>' --effect '<what it changes>'
```

To answer a question, rewrite its row in the whole Open Questions section:
the answer, the date, and status Answered. An approve command or a
`--delivery` answer marks the rows that asked for it Answered by itself and
prints "Marked Q-xx Answered"; do not edit those rows again.

## 8. Editing a record directly

- Prefer `toolkit work edit`. It works in every tracker the CLI drives and
  keeps the CLI's record of what it wrote.
- A local record's body text may also be changed with the file edit tool. The
  post-tool hook checks the record after the edit.
- Never change the header fields with a file edit, and never create a record
  with one. The pre-tool hook refuses both, because they would skip the
  approval gates.
- Never write a record from the shell: no `cat >`, `tee`, `sed -i`, `cp`, and
  no Python or Node script. The hook refuses it, so it only wastes a step.
- A Notion item changes only through `toolkit work` commands. Never write its
  page with another Notion tool.

## 9. Titles

- A new item's title uses the owner's own words for the request. When you
  shorten them, say the title in one line in the reply ("I started WI-003,
  'Write a short project brief'.").
- To retitle an item, say the new title to the owner in one line first. Never
  retitle quietly.
  `toolkit work set <id> --title '<new title>'`

## 10. Generated files

Never edit these by hand or from the shell. The hooks refuse it.

- `.work-items/DASHBOARD.md`: rebuilt by every `toolkit work` write and by
  `toolkit work sync`.
- `.work-items/.toolkit-state.json`: the id-to-path map and the highest id
  used.

## 11. Examples

An Open Questions row for a content question the owner must answer:

```markdown
| Q-01 | What should the project brief cover: goals only, or goals, users, and scope? | P1-T01 | Open | owner |
```

A history note that records an owner's answer and says what it changes:

```text
toolkit work history WI-012 --note 'Owner said: "keep archived rows out of the export"' --effect 'R-02 updated; requirements approval asked again.'
```

A section edit in Claude Code: the command, then the text, then a line holding
only `EOF`, all in one shell command:

```text
toolkit work edit WI-012 --section 'Agreed goal' --set-file - <<'EOF'
Anyone on the team can export the monthly report as a CSV file that opens in Excel.
EOF
```

The same edit in Codex:

```text
toolkit work edit WI-012 --section 'Agreed goal' --text 'Anyone on the team can export the monthly report as a CSV file that opens in Excel.'
```

# Team roles and team size

What each helper role does and returns, and how to size a design or build
team for one work item.

The main agent sizes the team fresh for each item. The owner decides and
steers; he cannot judge which internal helpers a small item needs, so he is
not asked about the small team:

- The small team for the item's kind (the first row of each example table
  below): the main agent picks it and states it in one line ("Design team: one
  requirements analyst, one architect, one critic, and a researcher when a
  question is open."). No question.
- A larger team: the main agent proposes it, and the owner agrees or changes
  it before any agent starts, unless the item already records his
  team-arrangement answer from `work-delegate`. That answer saves a repeated
  question; it does not approve a product decision, a design, or a result.

## The roles

| Role | Agent | What it does | What it returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements analyst | `requirements-analyst` | Reads the requirements as one whole, inside the larger system, and walks the flow start to finish as the person who uses the result | Ready or not ready, then missing pieces, places not explicit end to end, wording a builder could misread, build details inside requirements, and drift from the Agreed goal, each with a fix |
| Researcher | `researcher` | Answers one bounded question from project evidence, official documentation, and community sources | An answer, then findings labeled official documentation, project evidence, or community claim, each with source and date |
| Design architect | `design-architect` | Writes or fixes one design option | The draft, and after each fix round a list of what changed by requirement |
| Design critic | `design-critic` | Checks one draft against every requirement and the writing rules | One verdict per requirement (satisfied, partly, not), then findings with fixes |
| Builder | `builder` | Builds one planned task in its own worktree and runs its checks | What changed, the tests run and their result, the commit on its branch, and anything it could not do |
| Acceptance checker | `acceptance-checker` | Checks a finished result against each acceptance check and the design's Acceptance checks, or a build plan before the build; never the agent that built it | One verdict per requirement (met, partly met, not met) with evidence, defects seen in the diff, and checks that could not run; for a plan, each finding by task id |

In Codex, each agent's full text is in the skill folder as
`references/agent-<name>.md`.

Narrower briefs for the same roles:

| Brief | When to add it | Given to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing-build survey | The project is not new and nobody in this session has read what exists for this area | A researcher: map what the current build does for these requirements, with file paths, and where it falls short of the goal |
| Domain specialist | The platform has its own method, for example `sf-architect-solutioning` in a Salesforce project | The main agent opens that skill and passes its findings to the architect |
| Experience walk | The requirements describe a flow with several steps or screens | The requirements analyst before design, and the critic after: walk the flow start to finish as that person and report where it breaks |

## How to size a team

Weigh, in the context of what is being built:

- how many requirements there are, and how many are unclear;
- how many systems, platforms, or teams the result touches;
- whether a build already exists, and how much of it the result changes;
- how many design options the owner wants;
- how much is unknown about the platform, the version, or the data.

Then pick a team, say why each role and count is there, and say how many
agent runs the first pass takes. Cut what the item does not need. A small
design still gets one requirements analyst and one critic: those two make the
design loop stop for the right reason. A design with no critic is allowed
only in a session with no agent tool, or when the owner said no to helpers.
Then the reply and the design's Notes say that no critique ran.

## Example teams for a design

Starting points, not rules.

| Item | Requirements analyst | Researchers | Architects | Critics |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small: up to 5 clear requirements, one platform, one option, nothing built yet | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Medium: 6 to 15 requirements, or two platforms, or two options, or an existing build | 1 | 2 to 3, one per open question, plus the existing-build survey | 1 per option | 1 |
| Large: more than 15 requirements, three or more platforms, three options, or a rewrite decision | 1, with the experience walk | 3 to 5, one per open question | 1 per option | 1 per option |

## Example teams for a build

| Item | Builders | Acceptance checkers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One task, or tasks that must happen in order | 0 (the main agent builds) or 1 | 1 |
| Several independent tasks | 1 per independent task, each with its own files (in Codex, each in a worktree the main agent makes first: `helpers.md`, section 2) | 1 |

## What the owner sees

The small team: one line naming it. A larger team: a short list of role,
count, and one line on what each reads and returns, and the question whether
to run it. The owner can cut, add, or change any role. Record the team, for a
design or a build, in the item's Notes > Decisions and context.

# The solution design process

The detail behind each `solution-design` step: the readiness checklist, the
way of working, the design record, research, the architect and critic loop,
drafts in each host, and approval. The design's section names are in
`work-item-format.md`, "Sections of `DESIGN.md`".

## Contents

1. Checklist before the design round
2. Are the requirements ready?
3. The way of working
4. The design record
5. Research
6. Design and critique
7. Drafts in each host
8. Save, present, and approve

## 1. Checklist before the design round

Work through every item in order. Tick each one only when it is true.

- [ ] **The requirements are read and understood**

        are read

        item

        apart from assumptions
  - [ ] Notes > Solution options and considerations are treated as ideas,

- [ ] **The requirements are ready to design from**

  - [ ] Every place a builder could misread the wording is listed, with the

  - [ ] Every requirement that does not fit the end-to-end experience is

  - [ ] Gaps were fixed in the requirements through `work-requirements`, not

  - [ ] "Requirements and design readiness" has one row per `R-xx`, with its

- [ ] **The way of working is agreed**

  - [ ] Built-in mechanisms first, or a specialized approach

  - [ ] Unresolved discussion is in Notes > Open design questions, and the

Only when every box is ticked does the design round (step 7) start.

## 2. Are the requirements ready?

For steps 1 to 3.

- Read the requirements against the whole end-to-end experience of the
  person who uses the result, inside the larger system. A requirement that
  seems out of place, contradicts another, or makes no sense in that flow is
  flagged in the first reply, with the reason.
- Answer three questions: Is anything missing? Is every requirement explicit
  end to end? Where could a builder misread it?
- Say plainly whether the requirements are ready. List what is still
  unclear. Use no score.
- Not ready: say so in the first reply, with each missing piece, unclear
  piece, and misreading risk, each with a proposed fix. Push back even when
  the owner wants to move on: a gap fixed in the requirements costs one
  question; the same gap found by the critic costs a design round, and found
  by a builder costs a build.
- The owner can overrule a flag. Record his ruling and reason in the design's
  Notes > Design changes during the interview, with the `R-xx` it concerns.
- Requirements not approved but the owner asked for options first: keep the
  open choices visible in the design, save it as proposed, and say the
  requirements approval is still needed. A `build` or `data-load` item keeps
  its stage: the CLI refuses stage 04 without the approval.

## 3. The way of working

For step 4.

The owner is one person who decides and steers; the agent runs the work. Ask
him at most one question here, with a recommendation and a one-line reason,
and only when the answer changes the design. Skip anything already answered.
Ask it in the reply text, never through a question tool.

1. **Interview or scan first.** The agent decides: the interview when the goal
   or the constraints are open, the scan when the requirements are detailed
   and the unknowns are technical. Say which in one line.
2. **Approach and options.** Default: the platform's built-in mechanisms
   wherever they meet a requirement, custom only where nothing built-in does.
   One option unless the owner wants more, or the requirements leave a real
   choice he should make; then ask how many and what differs (for example
   built-in only against custom, or least change against best long-term
   fit). This is the one question worth asking.
3. **The team.** The agent picks it from `team-roles.md` and states it in one
   line. The small team (one requirements analyst, one architect, one critic,
   and a researcher when a question is open) needs no question. Ask only when
   the team is larger than that, because it then costs noticeably more.

Record settled answers in the item's Notes > Decisions and context as they
come. The approach also goes into the design's "Constraints and assumptions"
table, with the owner as its source.

## 4. The design record

For step 5.

- `toolkit work design <id> --create` creates the design from the project's
  template (`.work-items/work-item-template/DESIGN.md` when present,
  otherwise the toolkit's copy of the model) in the item's one design home.
  For GitHub or Jira, start the design comment from `assets/DESIGN.md`.
- `toolkit work design <id>` prints the current design. Paste the parts each
  agent needs into its brief.
- The design's header fields (`work_item`, `status`, `approved`) are written
  by the CLI. Never edit them by hand.
- The template opens with a fill-in guide comment. Follow it and delete it,
  and delete the unused example rows and optional sections, as the guide
  says.
- Several options go under "Design options", each as its own
  `### Option A — <name>` section (then B, C), each with the same inner
  headings: Approach, End-to-end behavior, Requirement coverage, Technical
  shape, Tradeoffs and risks, Build order. With one option, remove "Option
  comparison" and keep the owner decision.

## 5. Research

For step 6.

One researcher per bounded question. Good questions: what the platform offers
built in for a requirement; the current version's limits; what people are
doing for this kind of problem; what an existing component in this
repository already does. Each finding comes back with a source, a date, and a
label. Findings that change the design go into "Sources and decisions that
affect the build".

Salesforce projects: open `sf-architect-solutioning` as the specialist for
platform facts (objects, Flows, Apex, permissions). It is a skill the main
agent runs, not an agent. It returns its findings to this design and starts
no second interview. Pass its findings to the architect.

A community claim shapes the design only after a check against official
documentation, the project's code, or a test.

## 6. Design and critique

For step 7.

- **Architect.** One per option. The brief holds the design's current text
  (What this design solves, Requirements and design readiness, What exists
  today, Constraints and assumptions, Notes), the requirements, the research
  findings, the way of working, and which option to write. It says plainly
  whether the requirements are ready and does not design until they are.
- **Critic.** At least one for every design, even a small one, and one per
  draft. Returns one line per requirement (satisfied, partly satisfied, not
  satisfied) with evidence, plus findings on the goal, unnecessary custom
  work, sources, and writing. The critic is skipped only in a session with
  no agent tool at all (no Agent tool in Claude Code, no `spawn_agent` in
  Codex), or when the owner said no to helpers. Then the reply and the
  design's Notes say that no critique ran.
- **Fix loop.** Give the critic's findings to the architect. The architect
  fixes the draft and lists what changed. The critic checks again. Repeat
  until every requirement is satisfied and nothing material remains.
  - A finding the architect and critic still disagree on after two rounds
    goes to the owner as one question, with both positions in two lines each.
  - A requirement no design can meet goes to the owner as a requirements
    question, not a design compromise.
  - Stop because the list is empty or the owner decided the rest, never
    because the loop is long. Start another round only for a named finding
    or a changed input.
- Keep the review position in the design's Notes > Current position and next
  step (open findings, next action), not a transcript of every round.

## 7. Drafts in each host

- **Claude Code.** The architect writes no file and returns its whole draft
  in its reply. Claude Code refuses `rm` outside the project, so a temporary
  folder could never be deleted. The critic's brief holds that draft, pasted
  in. For a fix round, paste the last draft and the critic's findings into
  the new brief. Save the merged design with `--set-file -` and the text on
  standard input.
- **Codex.** Make one folder for this design with `mktemp -d`. The
  architect's brief names its draft file in that folder, named for its option
  (`option-a.md`). The critic's brief names the same file. Save the merged
  file with `--set-file <path>`, then delete the files and the folder
  (`rm <file>`, then `rmdir <folder>`) before you ask the owner anything.
- **Never** a fixed name in the shared `/tmp` (such as
  `/tmp/wi002-option-a.md`: another project's WI-002 could overwrite it), and
  never a draft inside `.work-items/`, where a second `DESIGN.md`-shaped file
  confuses the design lookup.

## 8. Save, present, and approve

For steps 8 and 9.

- Merge the final drafts into one design text: the header and opening
  sections, one `### Option` section per option under "Design options", the
  Option comparison (with several options), the Recommendation, then Sources,
  the misreading table, and Notes. "Selected design" says "Pending owner
  decision." until he chooses.
- Save it as proposed and set the item waiting on the owner (`approvals.md`,
  "Design approval"). "Saved but not verified": lead the reply with it.
- Tell the owner: how many options, one sentence each, the recommendation and
  its reason, what he will see when it is done, the main risks, the build
  order, and the decisions that need him. The full design is in the item; say
  where in one line.
- His yes, or his choice of one option: run the design approval checklist in
  `approvals.md`. Write the chosen option into every subsection of "Selected
  design" and into "Build and verification plan" (Technical sequence, and
  Acceptance checks with one row per requirement). Keep "Diagrams" when the
  template has it. Remove every leftover prompt, including a line that still
  says the plan comes after the owner chooses. `work-check` reads these
  Acceptance checks, so an empty plan leaves the checker nothing to check.
- Keep each header line (`**Requirements:**`, `**Design status:**`, and the
  rest) on its own line, and leave the Design status line as it is. Only
  `toolkit work approve <id> --design --by <owner>` marks it approved.
- He wants changes: record them in the design's Notes > Design changes during
  the interview, run another fix round for the named changes only, and ask
  again.
- Lasting lessons the owner stated along the way go through `memory-save`.
  Decisions for the whole project go through `work-decide`. Working design
  Notes are not project memory.
- The design reads like the project's writing rules: common words, real
  names, no figurative language, and a term defined the first time it
  appears.
- A failed save: lead with "Not saved" and keep the unsaved text.

## 9. Changing an approved design later

- Any change to the text of an approved design gets a history note that says
  what changed and whether the owner must approve it again. A factual
  correction that changes no choice needs no new approval; say so in the
  note.
- A build that shows the design does not work: record what failed in the
  design's Notes, set the design back to proposed, and run a fix round for
  the affected parts. Then ask for approval again.
  `toolkit work design <id> --status proposed`
- A design that a new one replaces completely: mark the old text superseded.
  `toolkit work design <id> --status superseded`
